item.title: Quickstart on Linux
item.description:
This page takes you from nothing to a first job on Linux with the shipped stack file and the setup helper, from a signed release. It sets up one class, linux-default. Nothing is installed on a node by hand: the stack has a service that installs the runner on every node. The page explains little. Install on Linux with Docker Swarm has every step by hand with the reasons, and Concepts explains the model.

Note

This is a CircleCI Labs project. CircleCI support does not cover it. It is a 0.x release: a minor release can change your stack files, so read the release notes before you upgrade. It is tested against CircleCI cloud only. What is tested says how, and Security says what a job on a runner can reach.

Availability. One token proxy runs on a manager, and every runner API call goes through it. While the proxy or its manager is down, no new job starts, and Swarm restarts the proxy. Use three managers for a production cluster. This is not an autoscaling or high-availability product: the replicas are fixed, and the nodes are yours.

Before you start

  • A node with Ubuntu LTS, Docker Engine 24 or later, a clock on NTP, and outbound HTTPS. CI tests Ubuntu 26.04 on amd64 with real jobs, and the start of the stack on arm64, with probe jobs on a real arm64 runner on main. RHEL 8 or later is documented and not tested. ppc64le and s390x start under emulation only, and no job runs there. Prepare each node shows how to install Docker. Prerequisites has the details, and Sizing the CPU and memory.
  • Outbound HTTPS from the node to runner.circleci.com, circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com, circleci-tasks-prod.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com, your VCS host, github.com (the release download), and the registries for the images (Docker Hub). Egress hosts says what each is for, and What needs internet lists everything. A node without internet access does not work in this release.
  • An organization admin who accepted the CircleCI Runner Terms, in the web app or by using the CLI for self-hosted runners, as CircleCI documents.
  • The CircleCI CLI 1.4.0 or later on your workstation or on the node. Step 1 signs it in.
  • cosign 3.1.3 or a later 3.x (CI signs and verifies with 3.1.3, and earlier versions are not tested), and jq and curl, on the node, to verify the release.
  • A bash shell. Run the commands on the node with sudo, or as a user in the docker group. The docker group is equivalent to root, so limit it.

Replace <namespace> with your runner namespace, and <org> with your organization slug such as gh/my-org, or its UUID.

Steps

  1. Sign in, and check that your organization has a namespace. Each organization has one namespace, which orbs and runners share, and only CircleCI support can change it. If your organization publishes orbs, it has one. circleci namespace get <namespace> looks up a name that you know. If your organization has none, create it.

    circleci auth login
circleci namespace create <namespace> --org <org> # only when the organization has no namespace yet

  2. Create a resource class and a token for it. The command prints the token once, so keep it for step 5. Without --org, the CLI takes the organization of the git remote of the current directory.

    circleci runner resource-class create <namespace>/linux-default --org <org> --generate-token

  3. On the node, download a release, verify it, and unpack it. A release is the install path: its stack file names the token proxy image of that release by tag and digest, and the CircleCI job that made it signed the checksums with a keyless cosign signature. A git clone of a branch or a tag gets the stack files with the default image latest, which is not pinned. The token proxy image is ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy: ccilabs is the Docker Hub organization of CircleCI Labs, and the signature check, not the name, is the trust root (Verify the token proxy image).

    Set version once, to the number of the latest release without the v, and read its notes. The line below is a placeholder: with it unchanged, the download fails and nothing runs.

    version=X.Y.Z

    Then paste this block. It runs in a subshell with set -euo pipefail, so the first failing check ends it. The three checks are the signature, the ref in the certificate, and the checksum, and only a bundle that passes all three is unpacked.

    (
 set -euo pipefail
 base="https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm/releases/download/v${version}"
 curl -fsSLO "${base}/machine-runner-swarm-${version}.tar.gz" -O "${base}/SHA256SUMS" -O "${base}/SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json"

 # 1. the signature: the CircleCI project and pipeline definition of this repository signed SHA256SUMS
 cosign verify-blob SHA256SUMS --bundle SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json \
 --certificate-identity "https://circleci.com/api/v2/projects/7bbdbb66-6ba8-4f6c-982e-d4fb401ec257/pipeline-definitions/8b2a66db-3f28-5c80-88e4-03f4694b5b60" \
 --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://oidc.circleci.com"

 # 2. the ref: a job of any branch can sign with that identity, so the certificate must also say that the job ran for refs/heads/main
 # (the long string is the OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 followed by the value refs/heads/main)
 hex=$(jq -r '.verificationMaterial | (.certificate // .x509CertificateChain.certificates[0]).rawBytes' SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json | base64 -d \
 | od -An -v -tx1 | tr -d ' \n')
 grep -Eq '^([0-9a-f]{2})*2b0601040183bf30010e0411(0c|13)0f726566732f68656164732f6d61696e' <<< "${hex}" \
 && echo "signed for refs/heads/main" || { echo "NOT signed for refs/heads/main: stop"; exit 1; }

 # 3. the file: its checksum is in the signed list
 sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing

 # only a verified bundle is unpacked
 tar -xzf "machine-runner-swarm-${version}.tar.gz"
 echo "RELEASE VERIFIED"
)

    Continue only when the last line is RELEASE VERIFIED. Anything else, an error message or no output at all, means that the release is not verified: delete the downloaded files and start again, or ask in an issue. The ref check exists because the signing identity is the same for every branch, so the block looks in the certificate for the extension 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 (the OID in the long string) with the value refs/heads/main, and fails when a job of another branch signed the file. Verify a release explains the identity and what a valid signature does not prove, and How the signature works explains the ref check.

    Change into the unpacked bundle. The paths below are relative to it.

    cd "machine-runner-swarm-${version}"

  4. Check the node and create the Swarm. Choose one of two forks. A Swarm that listens on the loopback address cannot accept other nodes, so a trial cannot grow into a cluster without a new swarm init and new secrets. Decide now.

    • Trial, one node. The Swarm listens on the loopback address, so nothing is exposed and no other node can join. The runners and the token proxy share the node, so a job that escaped its container could read the class tokens: use it for a trial.

      sudo linux/setup.sh --check --swarm-init

    • Cluster. Check every node, create the Swarm on the first one with an address that the others can reach, join the rest, and label the manager that runs the token proxy. Open the inter-node ports first. The shipped Linux class overlays are encrypted, so a multi-node cluster also needs IP protocol 50 (ESP) between nodes (Encrypted class networks). A first cluster of one manager and two workers is enough to try it. A node needs nothing else: the stack installs the runner on each node that joins.

      sudo linux/setup.sh --check # on every node
sudo docker swarm init --advertise-addr <manager IP address> # on the manager
sudo docker swarm update --task-history-limit 2 # on the manager
sudo docker swarm join-token worker # prints the join command: run it on each worker
sudo docker node ls # on the manager: every node is Ready
sudo docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true <manager node name> # on the manager

      The label marks the node that runs the proxy, which holds every class token. Runner services never run on a node with this label, so jobs do not share a node with the tokens. With no worker, the runner replicas stay Pending. With one manager, the proxy runs there by default. With several managers, pin the proxy to the labelled one when you deploy in step 6: Where the proxy runs, and when it moves shows the variable. Keep one manager that you do not drain, because the proxy needs it.

      Run steps 5 to 7 on the manager. Refer to Multi-Node Clusters for labels, zones, quorum, and encrypted overlays.

  5. Create the Swarm secret for the token. The helper asks for it with hidden input and never prints it. The token goes to the token proxy only. Then create the placeholder that the runners read instead of a token: any value works.

    sudo linux/setup.sh --secret linux-default
printf %s machine-runner-swarm-placeholder | sudo linux/setup.sh --secret runner-placeholder

  6. Copy the stack directory, and deploy your copy. For a first run, change nothing in it. You review it later, and from here on you deploy your copy and never the shipped files. The directory holds the stack files and the two scripts that they ship as Swarm configs, which the stack files name next to themselves. A new release changes the shipped files, so an upgrade is a merge of your copy with the new files: Upgrade shows how.

    cp -r linux/stack deploy
sudo linux/setup.sh --deploy --stack-file deploy/runners.yaml

    This is the whole install. The service runner-distributor starts on every Linux node (a node that you label for the microVM add-on is the exception: it has its own copy), downloads the runner of CircleCI, checks its SHA-256, and makes it available to the runner services. A runner container that starts first waits up to 2 minutes for it. In a release bundle, the token proxy image is pinned by digest. The helper warns when MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE is not pinned by digest.

  7. Check that the runners are up and connected. docker stack deploy does not wait, so the replicas need a minute to start.

    sudo docker stack services runners
sudo docker service logs --tail 20 runners_runner-distributor
sudo docker service logs --tail 20 runners_linux-default
circleci runner instance list --org <org> --resource-class <namespace>/linux-default

    The runners are healthy when REPLICAS shows 2/2 for runners_linux-default (or fewer for Pending replicas) and 1/1 for runners_token-proxy, the distributor shows one task for each node and logs a line such as [ ok ] current -> versions/3.1.13, the log of the runners has no 401 or error lines, and the CLI lists an instance with the status online. The same list is in the web app under Runners.

  8. Run a job. Save the following as .circleci/config.yml in a project of your organization, replace my-namespace, commit, and push. The same file is examples/linux-hello.yml.

    version: 2.1

jobs:
 hello:
 machine: true
 resource_class: my-namespace/linux-default
 steps:
 - run:
 name: Show where this job runs
 command: |
 echo "runner: $CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME"
 echo "user: $(id -un)"
 if [ -e /tmp/hello-marker ]; then echo "the container was reused"; exit 1; fi
 touch /tmp/hello-marker
 echo "clean container: no marker from an earlier job"

workflows:
 hello:
 jobs:
 - hello

    Run the workflow twice. Both runs pass, because Swarm starts a new container for each job.

Sizing and Pending replicas

The shipped file reserves 4 CPUs and 8 GB of memory for the runners: two replicas of linux-default (2 CPUs, 4 GB each). The token proxy and the distributor reserve little. A replica needs its whole reservation free on one node. Leave about 1 CPU and 2 GB for the operating system and Docker. Size the limits has a table of every shipped class, with the CPU and memory of a replica, the default replicas, and what else it needs.

The cost of the project is your own hardware, plus the runner concurrency of your CircleCI plan: the replicas of all classes and the jobs that wait share the concurrency limit of your organization. Disk is not limited per container. Each finished job leaves a stopped container until Swarm prunes its task (the setup in step 4 keeps the last 2 for each slot), and the images take space too. This repository has no measurement of the disk that a job needs, so watch a node during a trial.

A replica that does not fit stays Pending. That is not an error: Swarm waits for room, the other replicas work, and docker service ps --no-trunc runners_<service> shows insufficient resources on 1 node. To fit a small node, lower deploy.replicas in your copy and deploy it again with the same command. The smallest useful test is replicas: 1 for linux-default, which needs 2 CPUs and 4 GB. Refer to A task stays pending for the other causes.

What you did not do

The helper checks the node, starts Swarm, creates the secrets, and deploys the stack. It does not install Docker, create classes or tokens, edit the stack file, label or join nodes, or build images. It does not install the runner either: the runner-distributor service of the stack does that on every Linux node. Optional: use the setup helper lists each step.

Next

  • Install on Linux with Docker Swarm: the same steps by hand, RHEL, and the release verification.
  • Resource Classes: add classes, and change sizes and replica counts. linux-java and linux-hardened are in linux/stack/classes-extra.yaml; deploy that file with an extra -c together with runners.yaml. A class is a service, its token secret <service>-token and its network, and the secret and the network are also listed on token-proxy, which finds its classes in its secrets: there is no variable to set.
  • Security: choose between the default and the hardened class before you give a class to a team, and read what a job on a cloud node can reach.
  • Operations: pin or roll back the runner version, rotate tokens, and run the cluster.

item.title: Quickstart on Windows Server
item.description:
This page takes you from nothing to a first job on one Windows Server node with the shipped stack file and the setup helper, from a signed release. It explains little. Install on Windows Server with Docker Swarm has every step by hand with the reasons, and Concepts explains the model. Nothing is built and nothing is installed on the host: the service uses the stock Server Core image, and the distributor service of the stack installs the runner and Git.

Note

This is a CircleCI Labs project. CircleCI support does not cover it. It is a 0.x release: a minor release can change your stack files, so read the release notes before you upgrade. It is tested against CircleCI cloud only. What is tested says how, and Security says what a job on a runner can reach.

Availability. One token proxy (token-proxy-windows) runs on a manager, and every runner API call goes through it. While the proxy or its manager is down, no new job starts, and Swarm restarts the proxy. This page sets up one host, which runs the proxy and the jobs together: use it for a trial. This is not an autoscaling or high-availability product: the replicas are fixed, and the nodes are yours.

Before you start

  • A Windows Server 2022 or 2025 host that is not a domain controller, amd64, with a clock on NTP and outbound HTTPS. CI tests both versions with real jobs. Windows Server 2019 is not tested.
  • Docker Engine and CLI 28.0 or later in Windows-container mode (the stack files mount a subpath of a volume; .\windows\Setup.ps1 checks the version), and the Windows Containers feature, which needs a reboot. The Install-DockerCE script in the helpful_tools directory of the Microsoft Windows Containers repository installs both (Prerequisites has the details). The first pull of the servercore base image is about 2.2 GB and takes minutes to tens of minutes, depending on the network (about 10 minutes on the CI machines). Refer to Sizing for the CPU and memory.
  • Outbound HTTPS from the host to runner.circleci.com, circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com, circleci-tasks-prod.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com, your VCS host, github.com and release-assets.githubusercontent.com (the release, Git, and 7-Zip), mcr.microsoft.com, and Docker Hub. Egress hosts says what each is for, and What needs internet lists everything. A host without internet access does not work in this release.
  • An organization admin who accepted the CircleCI Runner Terms, in the web app or by using the CLI for self-hosted runners, as CircleCI documents.
  • The CircleCI CLI 1.4.0 or later. It can run on your workstation. Step 1 signs it in.
  • cosign 3.1.3 or a later 3.x on the host, to verify the release (CI signs and verifies with 3.1.3, and earlier versions are not tested). Install cosign shows how.
  • An elevated Windows PowerShell 5.1 session on the host for the steps that start with docker or .\windows.

Replace <namespace> with your runner namespace, and <org> with your organization slug such as gh/my-org, or its UUID.

Steps

  1. Sign in, and check that your organization has a namespace. Each organization has one namespace, which orbs and runners share, and only CircleCI support can change it. If your organization publishes orbs, it has one. circleci namespace get <namespace> looks up a name that you know. If your organization has none, create it.

    circleci auth login
circleci namespace create <namespace> --org <org> # only when the organization has no namespace yet

  2. Create the resource class and its token. The command prints the token once, so keep it for step 6.

    circleci runner resource-class create <namespace>/windows-default --org <org> --generate-token

  3. On the host, download a release, verify it, and unpack it. A release is the install path: its stack file names the token proxy image of that release by tag and digest, and the CircleCI job that made it signed the checksums with a keyless cosign signature. A git clone of a branch or a tag gets the stack files with the default image latest, which is not pinned. The token proxy image is ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy: ccilabs is the Docker Hub organization of CircleCI Labs, and the signature check, not the name, is the trust root (Verify the token proxy image).

    Set $version once, to the number of the latest release without the v, and read its notes. The first line is a placeholder: with it unchanged, the download fails and nothing runs.

    $version = 'X.Y.Z'
$base = "https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm/releases/download/v$version"
$zip = "machine-runner-swarm-$version.zip"

    Then paste this block. It stops at the first failing check, and only a bundle that passes all three checks (the signature, the ref in the certificate, and the checksum) is unpacked.

    & {
 $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
 foreach ($f in $zip, 'SHA256SUMS', 'SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json') { Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri "$base/$f" -OutFile $f }

 # 1. the signature: the CircleCI project and pipeline definition of this repository signed SHA256SUMS
 cosign verify-blob SHA256SUMS --bundle SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json `
 --certificate-identity 'https://circleci.com/api/v2/projects/7bbdbb66-6ba8-4f6c-982e-d4fb401ec257/pipeline-definitions/8b2a66db-3f28-5c80-88e4-03f4694b5b60' `
 --certificate-oidc-issuer 'https://oidc.circleci.com'
 if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'the signature does not verify: stop' }

 # 2. the ref: a job of any branch can sign with that identity, so the certificate must also say that the job ran for refs/heads/main
 # (the long string is the OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 followed by the value refs/heads/main)
 $material = (Get-Content -Raw -LiteralPath SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json | ConvertFrom-Json).verificationMaterial
 if ($material.certificate) { $cert = $material.certificate.rawBytes } else { $cert = $material.x509CertificateChain.certificates[0].rawBytes }
 $hex = -join ([Convert]::FromBase64String($cert) | ForEach-Object { $_.ToString('x2') })
 if ($hex -notmatch '^([0-9a-f]{2})*2b0601040183bf30010e0411(0c|13)0f726566732f68656164732f6d61696e') { throw 'NOT signed for refs/heads/main: stop' }

 # 3. the file: its checksum is in the signed list
 $want = ((Get-Content SHA256SUMS | Where-Object { $_ -match "\s$([regex]::Escape($zip))$" }) -split '\s+')[0]
 if ((Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath $zip).Hash.ToLower() -ne $want) { throw "the checksum of $zip is not the signed one: stop" }

 # only a verified bundle is unpacked
 Expand-Archive -LiteralPath $zip -DestinationPath .
 'RELEASE VERIFIED'
}

    Continue only when the last line is RELEASE VERIFIED. Anything else, an error message or no output at all, means that the release is not verified: delete the downloaded files and start again, or ask in an issue. The ref check exists because the signing identity is the same for every branch, so the block looks in the certificate for the extension 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 (the OID in the long string) with the value refs/heads/main, and fails when a job of another branch signed the file. Verify a release explains it, and How the signature works has the details.

    Change into the unpacked bundle. The paths below are relative to it.

    cd "machine-runner-swarm-$version"

  4. Pull the base image before you create the Swarm, because the network of the host drops for a few seconds after docker swarm init. A Server 2025 host runs this ltsc2022 image too.

    docker pull mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022

  5. Copy the stack directory. For a first run, change nothing in it. You review it later, and from here on you deploy your copy and never the shipped files. The directory holds the stack files and the script that runners.yaml ships as a Swarm config, which the file names next to itself. A new release changes the shipped files, so an upgrade is a merge of your copy with the new files: Upgrade says how.

    Copy-Item -Recurse windows\stack deploy

  6. Run the helper. It creates the Swarm, labels the node with the image tags it can run (the node is a manager, where the token proxy runs by default, so it needs no other label), asks for the token with hidden input, creates the secrets windows-default-token (the token proxy holds it) and runner-placeholder-token (what the runners read), and deploys your copy. Use the IPv4 address of the host. This is the whole install: the service runner-distributor-windows downloads and verifies the runner that the stack pins (the newest version that CI tests) and the pinned portable Git on its own, and Swarm pulls the token proxy image of this release by its digest.

    .\windows\Setup.ps1 -InitSwarm -AdvertiseAddr <host IPv4 address> -Class windows-default -StackFile .\deploy\runners.yaml -Deploy

  7. Check that the runners are up and connected, and then run a job. docker stack deploy does not wait, so the replicas need a few minutes to start: the first download of the distributor takes a while, the first runner tasks fail until it is done and are started again every 10 seconds, and the first task also pulls the image if you skipped step 4. docker service logs runners_runner-distributor-windows shows the install.

    docker stack services runners
circleci runner instance list --org <org> --resource-class <namespace>/windows-default

    The runners are healthy when REPLICAS shows 2/2 (or fewer for Pending replicas) and the CLI lists an instance with the status online. The same list is in the web app under Runners. Then save the following as .circleci/config.yml in a project of your organization, replace my-namespace, commit, and push. Run the workflow twice.

    version: 2.1

jobs:
 hello:
 machine: true
 resource_class: my-namespace/windows-default
 steps:
 - run: echo "computer $COMPUTERNAME, instance $MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_INSTANCE_ID"

workflows:
 hello:
 jobs:
 - hello

    The two runs print different values, because Swarm starts a new container for each job. The file examples/windows-job.yml has more steps.

Two things that differ from Linux

  • A job on Windows runs as an administrator. In a single-task class such as windows-default, the runner container holds only a placeholder, and the class token is in the service token-proxy-windows. A job can read the placeholder, and it may be able to send packets with a forged source address, because a Windows container cannot drop NET_RAW the way a Linux one can. This is not tested on Windows, and Security says what it could gain. The windows-persistent class is the exception: its container holds the real token, and a job can read it. Treat each class as a trust boundary. Refer to Token model on each OS.
  • A stop of a busy container from outside, such as an update, a scale-down, or a node drain, kills its job after about 5 seconds. A job that finishes ends its container cleanly. Change a Windows class while it is idle. Refer to Stop a busy Windows container.

Sizing and Pending replicas

The shipped file runs two replicas of windows-default, and each reserves 2 CPUs and 4 GB of memory, so the service needs 4 CPUs and 8 GB. The distributor and the token proxy set limits and reserve nothing (1 CPU and 1 GB, and 1 CPU and 512 MB), so leave room for them and for the operating system. The Windows engine rejects a CPU limit above the CPU count of the host. A replica needs its whole reservation free on one node. Size the limits has a table of every shipped class. The cost of the project is your own hardware, plus the runner concurrency of your CircleCI plan, and the disk is not measured here: the base image alone is about 2.2 GB, and every finished container keeps its layer until Swarm prunes it.

A replica that does not fit, or that no node is allowed to run, stays Pending. That is not an error: Swarm waits, and the other replica works. docker service ps --no-trunc runners_windows-default shows the reason, such as insufficient resources or scheduling constraints not satisfied. For a small host, lower deploy.replicas in your copy and deploy it again. Refer to A task stays pending for the other causes.

What you did not do

The helper starts Swarm. It does not install Docker or the runner, create classes or tokens, edit the stack file, label nodes for the optional classes, or build images. Optional: use the setup helper lists each option.

Next

  • Install on Windows Server with Docker Swarm: the same steps by hand, with the release verification.
  • Images: add your own tools on top of Server Core.
  • Security: the token model and BitLocker.
  • Operations: upgrade, rotate tokens, and run the cluster.

item.title: Concepts
item.description:
This page explains the model behind the stack files in this repository. Read it before you change a stack file or choose between the default and the hardened class.

The stack runs CircleCI machine runner 3 as Docker Swarm services. Swarm handles replicas, restarts, secrets, and placement. This repository adds only a stack file for each operating system, a small entrypoint and a runner distributor service for Linux, and optional setup helpers.

Services are resource classes

Each Swarm service is one CircleCI resource class. The service name is the short name of the class, so the service linux-default serves the resource class <namespace>/linux-default. A job selects the class in its config:

jobs:
 build:
 machine: true
 resource_class: <namespace>/linux-default

Each service also has one Swarm secret named <service>-token. The secret holds the token of that class. The single-task classes do not mount it in their runners: the token proxy holds it and adds it to the claims of the runners of that class, so a runner can only claim jobs for its own class. A runner holds a made-up placeholder. A persistent class mounts its token in the runner container itself.

flowchart TB
nodes["Nodes: Linux amd64, Linux arm64, Windows<br/>Labels decide where tasks may run"]
subgraph services["Swarm services: one for each resource class"]
direction LR
s1["linux-default<br/>replicas: 2"]
s2["linux-python<br/>replicas: 1"]
s3["windows-default<br/>replicas: 2"]
end
r1["container 1"]
r2["container 2"]
r3["container 1"]
r4["container 1"]
r5["container 2"]
api["runner.circleci.com<br/>Runners connect outbound over HTTPS 443 only"]
nodes --> services
s1 --> r1 & r2
s2 --> r3
s3 --> r4 & r5
r1 & r2 & r3 & r4 & r5 --> api

The runner containers poll CircleCI for work. Nothing connects to a runner, so the stack publishes no ports.

The token proxy

The service token-proxy of the Linux runners.yaml (on Windows token-proxy-windows of the Windows runners.yaml, which works the same way, with the differences in Windows: Windows has no NET_RAW drop, and nothing there is tested for a forged source address) keeps the class tokens away from the runners and their jobs. A runner sends its API calls to the proxy (CIRCLECI_RUNNER_API_URL: http://token-proxy:8080) and holds only a made-up placeholder token. The proxy adds the class token to one call, the task claim, and passes every other call on to CircleCI. The runner and its task agent use the task token from the claim response for the rest.

flowchart LR
subgraph cls["Class overlay networks"]
r1["linux-default runners<br/>placeholder token"]
r2["linux-python runners<br/>placeholder token"]
end
p["token-proxy<br/>one replica<br/>holds every class token"]
api["runner.circleci.com"]
r1 -- "claim, task calls" --> p
r2 -- "claim, task calls" --> p
p -- "HTTPS: the class token on the claim only" --> api

The proxy decides who may claim from the network and not from what a runner says. It allows a claim only from an address that Swarm DNS lists now for tasks.<service> of a class, once for each container, and gives it the token of that class. A container that is not a runner, or a runner that claims a second time, gets 403. A claim whose outcome is unknown (the request reached CircleCI and the answer was lost) counts as a claim, so the proxy fails closed. For this the proxy is attached to the overlay network of every class, runs with endpoint_mode: dnsrr so that it sees the real source address, and the runners drop NET_RAW so that they cannot forge one. Refer to The token proxy for what it protects and what it does not, and to Monitor the token proxy for what happens when it is down.

What this changes for you:

  • Secrets. You create the class secrets <service>-token as before, and one more secret, runner-placeholder-token, with a made-up token. Only the proxy mounts the class secrets. Every runner mounts the placeholder.
  • Classes. A new single-task class needs two lines in the proxy: its network (Linux) and its secret <service>-token, which the proxy takes as a class named <service>. Refer to Resource classes. The persistent classes do not use the proxy.
  • The image. The proxy is a static Go binary in a published container image, ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy on Docker Hub (ccilabs is the Docker Hub organization of CircleCI Labs, and the signature is the trust root, not the name), on a minimal base: no shell, uid 65534 on Linux, a read-only root file system. One tag covers Linux amd64, arm64, ppc64le and s390x, and Windows Server 2022 and 2025 (amd64). The service token-proxy pulls it by itself, so no distributor installs it. A release bundle names the image of its release by tag and digest, and a checkout names latest, which only a release moves. Every digest is signed. Refer to The token proxy image and Verify the token proxy image.
  • The state. The proxy keeps the addresses of the runners that have claimed in the small volume proxy-state, on the node that it runs on: a manager by default. A restart on that node refuses only the runners that claimed, and a runner that started before the proxy is never locked out. If the proxy moves to another node, the state stays behind: refer to Where the proxy runs, and when it moves. In a cluster, label the node that runs the proxy machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true: runner services never run on a node with that label, so jobs do not share a node with the proxy. On a single node, set no label. With several managers, the label and a placement variable pin the proxy to one.

Add-on stack files and how they merge

Each operating system has one main stack file, runners.yaml, that defines the default classes and deploys on its own. The optional classes live in add-on stack files next to it: persistent.yaml, docker-build.yaml, and ssh-rerun.yaml on both systems, custom-image.yaml on Windows, and microvm.yaml and the prototype container-mode.yaml on Linux (MicroVM jobs, Container mode). container-mode.yaml adds one service, the container agent, that runs Docker-executor jobs for the classes in its settings, with a secret for each. An add-on stack file is not a patch of the main file. It defines services of its own, and each service needs its own resource class and its own <service>-token secret. The one exception on Linux is the token-proxy service: docker-build.yaml, ssh-rerun.yaml, and microvm.yaml also add their classes to it (a network, a secret, and a variable), so deploy them together with runners.yaml. persistent.yaml and container-mode.yaml do not touch the proxy: they keep their own tokens.

docker stack deploy -c runners.yaml -c persistent.yaml runners reads the files in the order given and merges them into one stack, as Docker Compose does for several -f files. A service, network, secret, or volume that only one file defines is added, and a key that several files set takes the value of the later file. The shipped add-on stack files only add services. YAML anchors work inside one file only, so each add-on stack file repeats the common service settings, and a change to one of them goes into every file that you use.

Pass the same list of files, in the same order, on every deploy. Swarm updates the services of the files you name. The services of a file you leave out stay as they are and stop following your edits, and --prune removes them. Check a merge without a Swarm with docker stack config -c runners.yaml -c persistent.yaml.

Replicas set the concurrency

deploy.replicas is the number of runners in the class, and so the number of jobs the class runs at the same time. A replica that cannot fit on any node stays in the Pending state until capacity is free. Refer to Resource Classes for sizing and for choosing the count.

Single-task and continuous mode

Machine runner 3 has two modes. The stack files set the mode with the CIRCLECI_RUNNER_MODE environment variable.

Mode Value Behavior Environment
Single-task single-task (default in every stack file) The runner claims one job, runs it, and exits. Swarm starts a new container for the next job. Clean for every job
Continuous continuous (persistent classes only) The runner stays up and claims job after job in the same container. Shared by all jobs on that runner

Use continuous mode only for trusted projects that need warm caches. The optional persistent classes are the only services that use it. Refer to Persistent mode.

Job lifecycle

Swarm never reuses a container. Every exit, whether a finished job, an idle timeout, or a crash, leads to a new task and a new container because the restart policy is condition: any.

sequenceDiagram
participant S as Swarm
participant C as Container
participant A as runner.circleci.com
participant N as New container
S->>C: start a task from the image
C->>A: poll for a job (single-task mode)
A-->>C: claim one job
C->>C: run the job in a clean container
C-->>S: runner exits, container stops
Note over S: restart_policy any, delay 10s
S->>N: create a NEW task and container
N->>A: poll for the next job

The steps in order:

  1. Swarm starts a container from the service image. On Linux the entrypoint checks the runner, sets up the users, and starts the runner. On Windows the runner is the main process.
  2. The runner downloads its task agent, polls CircleCI, and claims one job.
  3. The runner steps the job down to the job user on Linux, runs it, and exits when the job ends.
  4. Swarm sees the exit, waits for the restart delay of 10 seconds, and starts a new container.

Three timing facts follow from this design:

  • A replica needs about 10 seconds plus container start-up before it can claim the next job. The other replicas of the class keep claiming jobs in the meantime.
  • Every new container downloads the task agent from circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com. Allow this host in your egress rules.
  • A single-task runner that finds no job exits after CIRCLECI_RUNNER_IDLE_TIMEOUT, which is 1h in the stack files. Swarm replaces it, so idle replicas pick up a rotated secret or a new image within an hour.

Stopping a service sends SIGTERM to the runner. The runner drains (a runner drain), which means it accepts no new job and lets the running job finish. The stack sets stop_grace_period: 5h5m, which is the runner max_run_time of 5 hours plus 5 minutes.

On Windows, stop_grace_period does not hold a busy container: a stop from outside kills its job after about 5 seconds. A finished job ends its container by itself, so only an update, a scale-down, or a node drain is affected. Change a Windows service while its class is idle. Refer to Stop a busy Windows container.

What a clean environment covers

A clean environment means that a job starts in a container created from the image, with nothing left by an earlier job.

Covered Not covered
Files and installed packages anywhere in the container filesystem Anything on a mounted volume: persistent classes keep a named volume by design
The home directory, /tmp, and the working directory The Docker engine of the node when a class mounts its socket or named pipe: images, containers, and build cache persist
Processes, environment variables, and shell history State outside the node, such as databases, registries, and shared storage
Users, groups, and sudo rules created by an earlier job The kernel: all containers on a node share it
On Windows, the registry, the user profile, %TEMP%, and C:\ProgramData Data of finished containers that Swarm has not yet pruned from the node disk

The runner is mounted read-only, so a job cannot change what the next job runs. On Linux it comes from the per-node volume runner-bin, which a service of the stack fills. Refer to The runner distributor on Linux. On Windows it comes from the same volume, filled by the service runner-distributor-windows, through two links that Docker resolves when it creates a container. Refer to The runner distributor on Windows. A new runner version is a new directory and a moved link, so the next job runs the new version, and a job that runs now finishes on the old one. Refer to Upgrade the runner.

The working directory needs no cleanup in a single-task class, because the container is discarded. On Linux, the runner does not clean it at all. The runner user cannot remove files that the job user owns, so the stack sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR to "false". Refer to Working directory cleanup.

Containers are not a virtual machine boundary. Read Security before you run untrusted code.

The runner distributor on Linux

The Linux services use stock images such as cimg/base, and the image holds none of the runner. The service runner-distributor puts the runner on every Linux node that runs the classes of runners.yaml, so nothing is installed on a node by hand. docker stack deploy is the whole install, and it is the only upgrade path.

  • The service. runner-distributor is a global service, so it runs on every Linux node, on a Docker-build node too, and on a node that joins later, except a microVM node (machine-runner-swarm.microvm=true): the microVM classes download their own runner into each VM (MicroVM jobs). It runs the stock alpine:3 image, pinned by digest. Its script, linux/stack/runner-distributor.sh, is a Swarm config.
  • The volume. The distributor writes to runner-bin, a named volume that exists once on every node. Each version has a directory versions/<version> with bin/circleci-runner, SHA256, VERSION, and TARBALL. The link current points to the active version and moves with one atomic rename. The file history lists the versions in the order they were active.
  • The runner services. Every class mounts runner-bin read-only at /opt/machine-runner-swarm. The entrypoint is another Swarm config, mounted at /circleci-runner-entrypoint with the mode 0555, and it starts as root. A job cannot change either of them.
  • Not the token proxy. The distributor installs the runner only. The token proxy is an image that Swarm pulls: refer to The token proxy.
  • The wait. The entrypoint waits up to MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_WAIT seconds (default 120) until current exists, so a first deploy and a new node need no order. Then it resolves current once, when the container starts, and checks the binary against its record. Without a runner, or with a binary that differs, it exits with code 80, and Swarm tries again after the restart delay.

Because a container resolves current once, a running job and its container keep their version. The next container, which is the next job, gets the new one. A persistent class runs one container for all jobs, so it picks up a new version when its container restarts. Refer to Recycle a class.

The runner services carry no version and no hash. Which version the nodes run is a setting of the distributor service only, so an upgrade, a pin, and a rollback change that one service, and the runner services never restart. An idle replica keeps the old binary until it recycles, which takes at most the idle timeout of 1 hour.

Setting Behavior
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=3.1.13 (an exact version, the default: the newest that CI tests) The distributor pins that version, and checks the tarball against the SHA-256 values that the stack file carries for it, not against the manifest. It never changes by itself, it makes no request once the version is installed, and it switches to an installed version without any network, so a rollback needs no download. A release of this repository bumps the version and its SHA-256 values together
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=3.1 or 3 A floating line: the newest 3.1.x, or the newest 3.x.y, of CircleCI’s manifest. The distributor looks again every 24 hours, ignores the default SHA-256 list of the pin, and trusts the hash of the manifest, which is weaker
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=current A floating value: CircleCI’s current release, within major version 3. It looks again every 24 hours, ignores the default list, and trusts the hash of the manifest

Like machine runner 3 and container runner, the runner version is chosen by the operator: an exact pin by default, a floating value on request. Refer to The version policy for the rules, and to how this compares with machine runner 3, container runner and the orchestrator.

The distributor verifies every download against a SHA-256 and records the SHA-256 of the binary next to it. Refer to Upgrade the runner on Linux for the settings and to Runner binary integrity on Linux for the checks.

The runner distributor on Windows

The Windows services use the stock Server Core image, and the image holds none of the runner and none of Git. The service runner-distributor-windows does what the Linux distributor does, with the same settings, the same version policy and the same rule that a runner service carries no version: docker stack deploy is the whole install, and the only upgrade path.

  • The service. A global service on the nodes with the label machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022, from the stock servercore:ltsc2022 image with process isolation. Its PowerShell script, windows\stack\runner-distributor.ps1, is a Swarm config.
  • The volume and the links. It writes to runner-bin: versions\<version> for the runner (with SHA256, TARBALL and VERSION), git\<git version> for portable Git, and two relative directory symbolic links, current and git\current. Every class mounts the volume read-only twice, with volume.subpath: current at C:\machine-runner-swarm, and git\current at C:\Program Files\Git, where the task agent expects tar.exe.
  • No entrypoint. circleci-runner.exe is the main process. A runner task that starts before the first flip fails and starts again after the restart delay, so a new node needs no order, and nothing checks the binary when a container starts. Refer to Runner binary integrity on Windows.
  • Not the token proxy. It installs the runner and Git only. The service token-proxy-windows runs the Windows image of the token proxy, which Swarm pulls: refer to The token proxy.
  • Locked files. Windows cannot replace or delete files that a running container uses. The distributor installs a version next to the others, flips the link, and removes an old version only when no container uses it. A running job keeps its version, and the runner services never restart, so no busy job is killed by an upgrade.

Refer to Upgrade the runner on Windows for the settings.

Users and the runner token on Linux

Inside each Linux container, two accounts exist:

  • The runner user circleci-runner (uid 2000) runs circleci-runner and owns the token file. It has no sudo rights and cannot write to /opt/machine-runner-swarm.
  • The job user runs every job step. It is circleci in the cimg images, or the account you name with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_USER.

The runner steps each job down to the job user with command_prefix: sudo -niHu <job user> -- in the default class, or setpriv when the image has no sudo, and always setpriv --no-new-privs in the hardened class. The token is never in the job environment, and the config file that the runner reads is readable only by the runner user and root. In the single-task classes, that file holds the placeholder: the class token is in the token proxy, not in the container.

What happens next depends on one setting, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO.

Class type Setting Jobs have sudo Can a job read the class token
Default (linux-default, and linux-java of classes-extra.yaml) MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO: "true" Yes, passwordless, as in the Docker executor No, the container holds a placeholder. Only a job that escapes the container onto the node of the proxy can
Hardened (linux-hardened of classes-extra.yaml) MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO: "false" No No, for the same reason
Persistent (linux-persistent, no proxy) MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO: "false" (the shipped file; "true" is the opt-in) No (with "true": yes) No, as in the hardened class. With "true", yes if the job uses sudo. Refer to The persistent class

The default class. Jobs keep the passwordless sudo that many orgs and orbs expect, for example sudo apt-get install. A job that uses sudo is root in its container: it can read the placeholder and the files of the runner, and become the runner user. It finds no class token. The test linux/tests/token.sh measures what the user of a job can read in the runner’s config file, and linux/tests/proxy.sh scans the containers as root and finds no class token.

The hardened class. The entrypoint steps every job down with util-linux setpriv --no-new-privs, even when the image has sudo, and edits no file of the image. Swarm ignores no-new-privileges, so setuid binaries such as sudo and su stay in the image, and the class keeps SETUID and SETGID for the step-down. The kernel flag that setpriv sets is inherited by the job and everything it starts and cannot be cleared, and it makes them ignore the setuid bit. The sudo of the image, with its rules intact, therefore cannot lift a job to root, and neither can any other setuid binary, even through a local-root bug. The job user then has no way to become root or the runner user, so the files and processes of the runner are out of reach of jobs. The container refuses to start if the image has no util-linux setpriv (exit code 80). The trade-off is that jobs cannot install system packages at run time, and that nothing in a job can gain privileges through setuid or file capabilities, for example ping or mount, so you build the tools into the image. CircleCI also recommends pre-installing dependencies as the most secure option. A kernel or container-runtime bug can still lift a job to root, because the containers share the host kernel.

Choose the hardened class for shared or regulated work. Choose the default class for a single trusted team that needs sudo. A stolen token lets its holder run a runner on that class and claim jobs, which exposes the code and secrets of those jobs, so the proxy matters more than the sudo setting. Refer to Security.

What the Linux entrypoint does

The entrypoint circleci-runner-entrypoint starts as root, prepares the container, and then runs the runner as the runner user. It never reads the token or the placeholder. In order, it:

  1. Waits for the runner distributor of the node, resolves the link current once, and checks the runner binary against its SHA-256 record. Then it checks that the runner and every directory above it, up to /opt/machine-runner-swarm, are owned by root and not writable by the group or others. Refer to The runner distributor on Linux.
  2. Looks for the tools it needs. sudo or util-linux setpriv steps jobs down, and setpriv or su starts the runner. With MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO=false, util-linux setpriv with --no-new-privs is required, whether or not the image has sudo. Without the tools it exits with code 80. Refer to What an image needs.
  3. Creates the users with useradd or adduser: circleci-runner with uid and gid 2000, and the job user when the image has none. It does not edit /etc/passwd by hand, because sudo refuses a user that has no passwd and no shadow entry.
  4. Sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_COMMAND_PREFIX. A value in the service environment does not override it.
    • With sudo, the prefix is ["sudo","-niHu","<job user>","--"]. The file /etc/sudoers.d/90-circleci-runner lets uid 2000 run commands as the job user only, keeps the PATH of the image, and keeps the environment variables of the image.
    • Without sudo, or with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO=false, the prefix is a setpriv command that gives the job no capabilities. In the hardened class it also carries --no-new-privs. It runs the job through env -u for every CIRCLECI_RUNNER_* and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_* variable of the container (the runner name stays), so the settings of the runner and the stack do not reach the job, as with the reset environment of sudo. The runner holds CAP_SETUID and CAP_SETGID as ambient capabilities only to call it.
  5. Creates the directories: the task agent directory, owned by uid 2000, and the working directory with its parent /var/opt/circleci, owned by the job user.
  6. Adds the job user to the group of /var/run/docker.sock when the class mounts the socket and the group is not root. Refer to Docker Builds.
  7. Runs the runner with exec as uid 2000. The init process of the container (init: true) passes SIGTERM to it, which starts the runner drain.

The entrypoint does not validate the runner name, the token, the mode, or the timeouts, and it has no guard against the reuse of a container. The runner checks its own settings and exits with code 80 for a bad one, and Swarm never reuses a container.

With sudo, a job gets the environment variables of the image, such as PATH, JAVA_HOME, and LANG, the variables you set in the service, such as a proxy, and CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME. It gets nothing else from the runner. The runner runs a few commands of its own, such as circleci-agent version, without the step-down, as the runner user.

Users and the runner token on Windows

Windows containers have no step-down. The runner and the jobs run as ContainerAdministrator, because the runner needs the symbolic link privilege of that account to install the task agent. A job can therefore read the config file of its runner. In a single-task class that file holds only the placeholder, and the class token is in the service token-proxy-windows. In the persistent class it holds the real token. The token is not in the job environment. A hostile job on the same host as the proxy can still reach the token, because process isolation is not a security boundary: refer to Windows.

Treat each Windows resource class as a trust boundary: use one token for each class, restrict who can use the class, and rotate tokens. The Linux variables MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_USER do not exist on Windows, and Windows ignores them. Refer to Token model on each OS.

Placement

Services carry constraints and nodes advertise capabilities. The built-in properties are node.platform.os and node.platform.arch. This repository adds the node labels machine-runner-swarm.zone, machine-runner-swarm.docker-build, machine-runner-swarm.microvm, machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022, machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025, and machine-runner-swarm.class.<service>. Refer to Multi-Node Clusters.

Why Swarm and not plain Compose

A plain docker compose up restarts the same container, so the environment is not clean. Swarm creates a new container for every task. The FAQ lists the trade-offs.

Glossary

Term Meaning
Stack file A Compose-format YAML file that docker stack deploy reads. Each OS has a main stack file (runners.yaml) and optional add-on stack files. This documentation never calls an add-on stack file an overlay, because an overlay network is a different thing
Stack The services that one docker stack deploy creates. The documentation names it runners, so the service linux-default is runners_linux-default in Swarm commands
Resource class, service A resource class is the CircleCI name, <namespace>/<name>, that a job selects with resource_class. A service is the Swarm object that runs it. One service serves one class, and the service name is the class name without the namespace
Replica, container A replica is one runner of a service, and deploy.replicas says how many. Swarm runs each replica as a task, which is one container at a time. When a job ends, the container ends, and Swarm creates a new task and container for the same slot
Node A host in the Swarm, a manager or a worker. Node labels and service constraints decide where a replica may run
Single-task mode, continuous mode The two modes of machine runner 3. Single-task runs one job and exits, which gives a clean environment. Continuous keeps the runner up for many jobs. Refer to Single-task and continuous mode
Persistent class A class that runs in continuous mode with a named volume, so jobs share state. It gives up the clean environment
Default class, hardened class The Linux default classes (linux-default, and linux-java of classes-extra.yaml) keep passwordless sudo for jobs. The hardened class (linux-hardened of classes-extra.yaml) steps every job down with setpriv --no-new-privs, so sudo cannot raise the job user. Refer to Users and the runner token on Linux
Token secret The Swarm secret <service>-token. It is a runner config file that holds the token of the resource class. The token proxy mounts it, or, in a persistent class, the runner does
Token proxy The service token-proxy of runners.yaml: it holds the class tokens of the Linux single-task classes and adds the token of a class to the claims of that class’s runners. Refer to The token proxy
Placeholder secret The Swarm secret runner-placeholder-token: a runner config with a made-up token, which every proxied runner reads instead of a real token
Entrypoint On Linux, the script circleci-runner-entrypoint, which a Swarm config delivers. It checks the runner, prepares the users, and then starts the runner. On Windows there is none: the runner is the main process
Runner distributor On Linux, the global service runner-distributor; on Windows, runner-distributor-windows (it installs portable Git too). On every node it downloads, verifies, and installs the runner into runner-bin, moves current, and looks again every MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CHECK_INTERVAL. Refer to The runner distributor on Linux
runner-bin The named volume, one on every Linux node, that holds the runner versions. The distributor writes it, and the runner services mount it read-only at /opt/machine-runner-swarm
current The link in runner-bin that points to the active versions/<version>. A container resolves it once, when it starts. As a value of MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION, current is one of the floating values (with 3.1 and 3): it makes the distributor follow CircleCI’s current release
Record The file versions/<version>/SHA256, which holds the SHA-256 of the binary in the format of sha256sum -c. The distributor writes it when it installs a version, and the entrypoint checks the binary against it at every container start
Setup helper The optional scripts linux/setup.sh and windows\Setup.ps1, which run steps of the install pages with checks. On Linux the helper checks the node, starts Swarm, creates secrets, and deploys. It installs nothing, because the distributor installs the runner
Stock image, custom image A stock image is a publisher’s image as it is, for example cimg/base or Windows Server Core. The stack mounts the runner into it, on Linux from the volume runner-bin and on Windows from the host. A custom image is one you derive from it, for example to add tools. Refer to Images
Drain The word has two meanings. A runner drain happens when the runner gets SIGTERM: it takes no new job and finishes the running one. A node drain is docker node update --availability drain: Swarm stops the tasks of that node, which starts a runner drain in each, and starts replacements on other nodes. This documentation always says which one
